The Bacciferous Herbs are the Chamcemorus ', Smilax aspera, Bryonia Alba and Nigra, Angelica Baccifera, Aconhum Racemo - sum, Solannm Racemofum Americanum, Hypogloffum, Laurus Alexandria, Oxymyrfine, Polygonatum, Li - liumConv allium, Monophyllon, Mandr agora, Herb a Paris, Solanum Lethale, Malum Infanum, Solanum Vulgare, Alfme Baccifera, Solanum Somniferum, Al - kpkengi, Asparagus, Vitis Idxi palluftris, See. Davis a iVelchman; and is a Sea Instrument of good use to take the Suns Altitude at Sea. It consists of Vanes A, BandC; and of two Arches. The Vane at A is called the Horizon Vane that at B the Shade Vane; and that at C the Sight Vane. The lesser Ark B is of Degrees, and that of C ( or fg ) of o Degrees. In time of Observe - tion the Shadow Vane B is fet upon the Arch just to an even Degree of some Altitude less than you judge the Complement of the Sun ’ s Altitude will be, by o or Degrees. The Horizon Vane is put on at A, and the Sight Vane on the th Ark fg; and then the Observer ’ s Back being turned to the Sun ( whence the Name of Back Staff or BackrQuadrant ) he lifts up the Instrument, and looks through the Sight Vane, riling or sal - ling the Quadrant till the Shadow of the upper Edge of the Shade Vane fall on the upper Edge of the Slit in the Horizon Vane; and if then you can see the Horizon through the said Slit, the Obfer - vation is well made: But if the Sea appear in - stead ot the Horizon, move the Sight Vane lower towards g: If the Sky appear, move it upwards towards /; and so try till it comes right. Then observe how many Degrees and Minutes are cut by that Edge of the Sight Vane, which an - sewers to the Sight Hole, and to them add the De - grees cut by the upper Edge of the Shade Vane t The Sum is the Sun ’ s Distance from the Zenith, or the Complement of his Altitude. To find the Meridian Altitude by this Instru - merit, you must continue the Observation as long as you perceive the Altitude to be - increasing; which you will find by the Sea ’ s appearing ( till through the Slit instead of the Horizon, and as you ! move the Sight Vane lower: But as soon as ever you see the Sky appear instead of the Horizon, the Altitude is then diminishing, and you must desist; and adding as before the Degree and Minutes on the two Arks together into one Sum, it gives the Sun ’ s Zenith Distance, or his Co - Altitude; and this fubftratfted from. leaves the true Altitude above the Horizon. That excellent Astronomer Mr. Flamfiead, con - tried a Glass Lens or double Convex to be placed in the Middle of the Shade Vane, which makes a small bright Spot on the Slit of the Horizon Vane, instead of the Shade: And this is a great Improve - ment, if the Glass be truly made, for by this Means the Instrument may be used in Hazy Wea - ther, and a much more accurate Observation made in Clear Weather, than could be by the Shadow. But after all, this Quadrant is by no Means so accurate as could be wished; and a large heavy Brass Astrolabe must needs be a much better Instrument.

bacule.c: BACULE ( in Fortification ) is a kind of Port - Cullis or Gate made like a Pit - fall with a Counter - poise, and supported by two great Stakes. ’ Tis usually made before the Corps de Gards advanced near the Gates.

badger.c: BADGER ( in Law ) is one that is Licenced to buy Corn or other Victuals in one Place, and carry it to another.

baileorbale.c: BAILE or Bale; the Seamen call lading or cass ing the Water by Hand out of a Boat Bailing, and when the Water is thus Bailed out, they fay, the Boat is freed. They call also those Hoops that bear up the Tilt of a Boat B ailes.

bailement.c: BAILEMENT ( a Term in Law ) signifying the Delivery of things, whether Writings or Goods, to another, sometimes to be delivered back to the Bailor, that is, to him that so delivers them, some - times to the use of him to whom they are deli - vered; and sometimes to a third Person.

bailiff.c: BAILIFF, is an Officer that belongs to a Man - nor, to order the Husbandry, and hath Authority to pay Quit - Rents issuing out of the Manner, fell Trees, repair Houses, &c. This Officer is he whom the ancient Saxons called a Reeve.

bailifferrant.c: BAILIFF Errant, is one that the Sheriff makes and appoints to go about the Country to execute Writs, to summon the Country Sessions, Assizes, &c.

bailifffranchises.c: BAILIFF Franchises, are those which are ap - pointed by every Lord within his Liberty, to do such Offices within his Precindls, as the Bailiff Er - rant doth abroad in the Country.

bailiwick.c: BAILIWICK, is the JurifdidHon of a Bailiff within his Lord's Franchise.

balani.c: BALANI, are certain Excrefences usually growing to the Shells of the larger forts of Sea Shell - Fifties.

balanus.c: BALANUS ( as it is called by some ) or Gians, is the Nut of the Yard covered with the Foreskin; sometimes the Clitoris is so called. It often also fig - nifies a Suppofirory. Blanchard.

ballandsocket.c: BALL and Socket, is an Instrument made of Brass, with a perpetual Screw to hold any Tele - scope, Quadrant, or Surveying Instrument, on a Staff for Surveying, Astronomical, or other uses.

ballanceorlibra.c: BALLANCE or Libra, is one of the Six Am - ple Powers in Mechanickj, which serves to find out the Equality or Difference of Weights in heavy Bodies. It is only a double Lever whose Hypomoch - lion is at the Centre of its length.
BALLANCE or Libra, is the Name of one of the twelve Signs of the zodiac / - into the first De - gree of which when the Sun comes, the Autumnal Equinox happens, and is the ith of September.

ballance.c: BALLANCE of a Watch or Clocks, is that part of it, which by its Motion regulates and deter -. mines the Beats: The circular Part of it is called the Rim, and its Spindle the Verge: There belongs to it also two Pallats or Nutts, which play in the Fangs of the Crown - wheel. In Pocket Watches that strong Stud, in which the lower Pevet of the Verge plays; and in the Middle of which one Pevet of the Crown - wheel runs, is called the Potans, or rather Potence: The wrought Piece which covers the Ballance, and in which the upper Pevet of the Ballance plays, is the Cock. The small Spring in siew Pocket Watches is called the Regulator '

ballast.c: BALLAST of a ship, is some heavy Matter, as Stones, &c. laid in the Hold next to the Keelfori or false Keel, in order to keep a Ship stiff, so that she may bear the more Sail. The Words about it are Trench the Baltajl, i. e. divide itinto two or more Parts. ballesterorballufler.c: BALLESTER, or Ballufler, in the Capital of the Ionick Column, is the lateral Part of the Scroll which makes the Curl - tuft.

ballista.c: BALLISTA, an ancient Warlike Engine to cast or shoot Darts or Stones, to batter and lHake City Walls. '

ballivo.c: BALLIVO amovendo, is a Writ to remove a Bailiff out of his Office, for want of diffident li - ving in his Bailiwick.

ballonorbalon.c: BALLON or Balon, is the French Word for a large Receiver or Vessel used in Chymistry, to re - weive what is distilled or drawn off by the Fire.

ballon.c: BALLON; in Architecture, is taken for around Globe, or top of a Pillar.

barkorbaraque.c: BARK or Baraque, is an Hurt like a little Cottare for Soldiers to lie in in the Camp: For - merly those for the Horse were called Bar achy, and those for the Foot Hum; but now Barack, is used for both indifferently. They are made usually when the Soldiers have no Tents, or when an Ar - my lies long in a Place in bad Weather, because they keep out Cold and W et much better than Tents. They are generally made by fixing four strong forked Poles in the Ground, and then lay - ing four others across them; then they buikf up the Walls with Sods, Wattles, or what the Place affords: The Top is either Planked or Thatched, or covered with Turf, as they have Convenience.

The Ingenious Mr. Haukjbee ( that invented the new Cupping - Glasses without Fire, now generally used: See his Air - pump ) hewed me a Baroscope where the Mercury rose and fell Inches with very great ease, and without breaking or dividing; and it may very easily be made for or. Inches, if a strait small thin Glass Tube can be blown and drawn of that length, and that it were as easily manageable. The Torricellian Experiment is made in a Tube of about Inches in length, with a small Ball, or rather Cylindrical Cavity on the Top; at the Bot - tom of this Tube, at A, is a very small Cistern with Mercury in it, and communicating with the ! free Air, into which the lower End of the Tube A B is put; then at a very Acute Angle, is the small Tube C D placed with its open Orifice in the aforesaid Cistern, and just under the Surface of the Mercury in it. And thus when the Atmosphere is high and heavy ( that is in dry and fair Weather ) the Mercury being pressed up into the Tube B A; leaves but little in the Cistern, and. Consequently there is but a little Weight of Mercury there, to press any out into the Tube CD, and consequent - ly then the Mercury will fall or descend towards C. But when in contrary Weather, the Mercury falls out of the Tube A B, there will be more in the Cistern, and consequently the Mercury must ascend further, or run higher up into the Tube CD And this is so tender and nice, that while I was in the Room, and looking on it, which was not above an Hour, the Mercury ascended near two Inches ( for Rain ) in the Hope Tube. One great Advantage; this Way of managing a Hoping Tube, seems to have above the Common One, which is, that the Mercury here moves all together in a Body, without breaking or dragging a Tail after it. Baroscope Statical: So Mr. Boyle calls an Instru - ment which he invented to estimate the Variations of the Air ’ s Gravity, and is thus describ ’ d. A very large and thin Glass Bubble ( of if such an one cannot be procured, or Smaller ones added together may do ) was counterpoised in a very tender Balance which would turn with the th Part of a Grain, and then all being. hung tip in a Frame, he found, that as the Air grew lighter and thinner, the Bubble would preponderate very manifestly; but when the A. ir grew thicker and denier, the Scale in which the Weights were would grow heavier, and mount up the Bubble. And this Effed he found would continue and an - fwer exactly to the rife and fall of the Mercury in the common Barometer or Baroscope. The Grounds on which this Noble Gentleman went in contriving thislnftrument, were these: . He considered, that though at first setting of it up, the Bubble and the Weights would be in ASquilibrio, because he carefully made them so; yet the Bulk of the Bubble did exceed that of the Metalline Counterpoise, by near times ( be it more or less, according tb the Specifick Gravity of the Weights used ) and therefore he confifiered, . That, according to the Laws of Hydrofta - Hicks, when two Bodies being of the fame also - lute Weight, but very different Bulks, come to be weighed in another Medium, they can no longer be equiponderant: For if the Medium be heavier or denser, the greater Body will be more buoyed up there than it was before, and constantly will a - bate of its Weight; but if the Medium should be lighter and rare, the contrary Effed would follow, and the Weight would be heavier than the Bubble. He considered also, that this must be the Case of the Air, whose Specifick Gravity is continually changing, according to the various Effluvia it re - chives from the Terraqueous Globe; and conse - quently, that it must needs be now denser, now rare, and accordingly more or less buoy up the Bubble. r Our Author hints, that this Instrument is capa - ble of several Improvements; and though in ma - ny Cafes the common Baroscope be preferrabie be - fore it, yet this hath some Advantages above That j as. L hat this is more parable than the other s sot many Persons can more easily get a Pair of good Scales and a Glass Bubble, than they can a Tube and Mercury for the common Baroscope; and this also is much more easily fitted up than that. This Statical Baroscope is alio much more easily carried from Place to Place. This Baroscope may be adjust - ed to the ordinary one, by finding what Weights answer exa & ly to every half Quarter of an Inch of the rife and fall of the Mercury; and these may help us to guess at the usual Variations of the Weather by ( hewing how much is wanting to bring the Scales to an Equilibrium. Also an Arch of a Circle, well graduated, may be fitted so as that the Tongue of the Balance shall play freely by it, and there ( hew the Change of, the Gravity of the Atmosphere, without the Ad - dition of any new Weights at all.

baseinfortification.c: BASE, in Fortification, is the exterior Side of the Polygon, d i. the Imaginary Line which is drawn from the Flanked Angle of a Bajlion to that which is opposite thereto.

baseofbasis.c: BASE of Basis, in Architecture, is the Foot of a Pillar that fuftaineth it, or that Part which is under the Body, and lies upon the Pedestal or Zocle when there is any: Therefore ’ tis hot used for the Lowest Part of a Column; but for all the leveral Ornaments of Mouldings which reach from Apophyges, of the riling of the Shafts of Pillars to the Plinth.

basefee.c: BASE FEE, or Base Estate, is a holding at the Will of the Lord.

basecourt.c: BASE COURT ( in Law ) is any Court that is hot of Record.

base.c: BASE of a Triangle: any one Side of a Triangle may be called the Base, but usually, and most properly that Side which lies parallel to the Hori - zon is taken for the Base. ’ Tis also the fame as to any other Right lin ’ d Figure.
BASE of any Solid Figure, is its lowermost Side, or that on which it stands.
BASE, of a Conick'ScBion ( if it have one ) is a Right Line in the Hyperbola and Parabola, arising from the common Intersection of the Secant Plane and the Base of ' the Cone.
BASE, the least fort of Ordnance, the Diame - ter of whbfeBoreis if - Inch, Weight Pound, Length Foot, Load Pound, Shot - Pound Weight, and Inch Diameter.

basering.c: BASE RING, of a Cannon, is the great Ring iiext behind the Touch - hole.

basepoint.c: BASE POINT, in an Escutcheon: See Efcut - pheon,

basetenure.c: BASE TENURE, or holding by Villanage or other customary Service, as distinguish ’ d from the Higher Tenure, in Capite, of by Military Ser - vice.

basilica.c: BASILICA, is the inner Vein of the Arm, cal - led Hepatica, the Liver Vein, it being the inferior Branch of the Axillaris, divided into Branches under the Tendon of the. Musculus PeSloralis.

BASILICA, in the Ancient Architecture, was i great Hall which had two Rapges of Pillars; and two Illes and Wings with Qalleries over them, These great Halls were at first made for the Pa - laces of Princes, afterwards they Were turned into Courts of Justice, and at last into Churches.

basilickconstitutions.c: BASILICK CONSTITUTIONS, were an A - abridgment and Reform of the Laws of Jufiinian ? made in the Reigns of Bafili'us and Leo ( whence they had their Name ) and were in force in the Eastern Empire till its Dissolution.

basilicuscorleonis.c: BASILICUS, Cor Leonis, a fix ’ d Star of the first Magnitude in the Constellation Leo; its Lon i gitude is A Latitude qo, z L Right A seen li - on Deg. Min.

basioglossum.c: BASIOGLOSSUM ( lee Hypjilogloffum ) is a Pair of Muscles that depress the Tongue: It arises Fleshy from the Balls of the Os Hyoides.

basisinanatomy.c: BASIS, in Anatomy, is the upper and broader Part of the Heart, opposite to the Mucro or Point t Also the Foundation of the Bone Hyoides. BASKETS of Earth: See Corbeills.

basisinmulick.c: BASIS, in Mulick, is the lowed of all the Parts thereof, which serves as a Foundation to the ou - pliers.

bassenceint.c: BASS ENCEINT, or Bass Enclosure, the fame with the Faujje Bray in Fortification, which fee.

bastion.c: BASTION; in Fortification, is now what was anciently called a Bulwarks It consists of two Faces ' as many Flanks, formerly a Gorge. It is usually made at the Angles of Forts, of a large heap of Earth, sometimes lined with Stone, but usually faced with Sods. The Lines terminating it are two Faces, two Flankj, and two Demigorges. The Union of the two Faces makes the outmost Angle / called the Angle of the Bajlion. The Union of the two Faces to the two Flanks, makes the Side Ah - gles called the Shoulders or Epaules; and the Uni - on of the two other Ends ol the Flanks to th two Curtains, forms the Angles of the Flanks.

BASTION with a Tenaille, whose Point is cut oft; and makes ah Angle inwards and two Points outwards: This is done when Water, &c. hin - ders carry ing the Bastion to its full extent, or when it Ihould be too ffiarp.

bastionssolid.c: BASTIONS Solid, are thole that have their Earth equal to the Height of the Rampart, without any void Space toward the Centre.

bastionsvoidorhollow.c: BASTIONS Void or Hollow, are those that have a Rampart and Parapet ranging only round about their Flanks and Faces; so that a void Space is left toward the Centre, and the Ground is there so low, that if the Rampart be taken, no Retrench - ment can be made in the Centre, but what will lie under the Fire of the Belieged.

bastioncomposed.c: BASTION Composed, is when the two Sides of the interior Polygon are very unequal, which makes the Gorges also unequal.. B ACTION Deformed, is that which wants one of its Demi - Gorges, because One Side of the Inte - rior Polygon is so very Iteorn MSTlz

bastiondemi.c: BASTION Demi, hath but on Face and Flank,, and is trivially before a Horn - work or Crown - work. This is also called an Efaulmcnt.

bastiondouble.c: BASTION Double, is that which on the Plain of the great Bastion hath another Bastion built higher, leaving iz or Feet between the Parapet of the lower and the Foot of the higher.

bastionflat.c: BASTION Flat, if the Distance between the Angles of the Interior Polygon be double the usual length, then a Bastion is made in the middle be - fore the Curtain but it generally hath this disard - vantage, that unless there be an extraordinary Breadth allowed to the Moar, the turning Angle of the Counterscarp runs back too far into the Ditch, and hinders the Sight and Defence of the z opposite Flanks.

bastionregular.c: BASTION Regular, is that which hath its due proportion of Faces, Flanks and Gorges. B ASTON, a Ft end vvord in Architecture, the fame with the Tore in Heraldry the fame with A button: Which fee.

bathmis.c: BATHMIS, is a Cavity in the Bone of the Arm or Shoulder, on each side one whereinto, when the whole Hand is stretched forth and bended, the Pro - cess of the undermost and lesser of the long Bones of the Cubit enters. This is also called Trochlea

batrachus.c: BATRACHUS, is a Tumour under the Ton - due, which makes Men croak like a Toad, when they speak. Blanchard.

battaile.c: BATTAILE, is an ancient Trial in our Law, which the Defendant in Appeal of Murder, Rob - very, or Felony, might chuse, that is, to fight with the Appellant, for proof whether guilty or not grown obsolete and wholly disused.

battalion.c: BATTALION, is a Body of Infantry of about,, or Men, of which usually f are Pikes in the middle, and the other f are Muskets polled on the WingS But the Number of Men is by no means certain. Battalions are usually drawn up fix deep, or with fix Men in File, or one before ano - ther those in length or side by side being called Ranks. Some Regiments consist of but one Bat - talon but when they are Numerous they are divided into several Battalions according to their Strength and so that every one may be about or. The Battalions of French Guards have com - monly but Companies, because each Company consists of Men. But of other French Regi - ments there go Companies to a Battalion, be - cause they are but Men in a Company. Of the Smfs Guards Companies make a Battalion, be - cause. each Company hath Men. When a Battalion is to be formed out of the Companies of several Regiments ina Garrison, &c. then those of the Eldest Regiments post themselves on the Right those of the Second on the Left, and so all other successively on the Right and Left, till the youngest fall into the Centre. The Subal - teran Officers take their Post before their Com - sanies, the Captains on the Right and Left accord - dg to their Degree. Battalions are divided into Divisions, thymus - queteers in the Right and Left, and the Pikes in the middle. In Marching, when there is ' not Room for so great a Front, they break into Subdvi - signs as the Way and Ground will allow. The great Art of drawing up a Battalion is to dispose it so as. that it may belt resell a Party of Horse in an open Field, and that itmay with ad - vantage engage with either Horse or Foot.

battery.c: BATTERY ( in Law ) is an A t that tends to the breach of the Peace of the Realm.
BATTERY en Echarp, is that which plays obliquely. n &
BATTERY ’ dRevers, or Murdering Battery, is one that bears upon the Back of any Place.

batteryinfotiftcation.c: BATTERY, in Fotiftcation, is a place raised on purpose where Cannon are planted, from thence to play upon the Enemy the Platform on which they are six'd being made of Planks that support the Wheels of Carriages, so as to hinder the Weight of the Cannon from sinking them into the Ground, and incline somewhat towards the Parapet to check the Recoiling of the Pieces.

batteries.c: BATTERIES of a Camp, are Places to plant great Guns on, and are usually surrounded with a Trench and Pallifadocs at the Bottom, as also with a Parapet on the top, having as many Holes as there are Pieces of Artillery - and with two Redouts on the Wings, or certain Places of Arms capable of covering the Toops that are appointed for their Defence. In all Batteries the open Spaces left to put the Muzzles of the great Guns out, are called Embra - sures, and the Diftafices between the Embrasures Merlons. The Guns are generally about iz Foot distant one some another, that the Parapet may be strong, and the Gunners have room to work.

batterysunk.c: BATTERY Sunk, or Buried, is when its Plat - form is funk or let down into the Ground so that there moist be Trenches cut in the Earth against the Muzzles of the Guns, for them to fire out at, and to serve for Embrasures. This fort of Battery which the French call En Terre, and Ruinate, is generally used on the first making of Approaches, to beat down the Parapet of any Place.

batteriescrop.c: BATTERIES Crop, are two Batteries which play athwart one another upon the fame thing, forming there an Angle, and beating with more Violence and Deftrudtion, because what one Bul - let Ihakes, the other beats down.

batteryenfilade.c: BATTERY Enfilade, is one which scourse or sweep the whole Length of a Strait Line.

batteryjoint.c: BATTERY Joint, or par Camerade, is when several Guns play at the fame time upon one Place.

batteurs.c: BATTEURS d ‘ Rftrade, or Scouts, are Horse - men sent out before, and on the Wings of an Ar - my, a Mile, or two, or three, to make Difcoveriesj which they give an account to the General.

battlements.c: BATTLEMENTS, are the Tops of the Walls of Buildings made in the Form of Embrasures and Merlons, as in Fortified Places.

battology.c: BATTOLOGY, is a vain and foolish Repetiti - on of the fame Words over and over again in any Discourse like the trifling Poet Battrn mentioned by Ovid, who introduces him saying, Month bus [ in quit ) erant & erantfub montibus Hits.

battooneaterm.c: BATTOONE, a Term in He - raldry, signifying a th Part of a Bendjinijler: It is the usual Mark of Illegitimacy, and is always born couped, or cut off after this manner. It also signifies the Earl Mar - shall's Staff.

bay.c: BAY, is a Term used by Geographers and Sea - faring Men, for an Arm of the Sea coming up in - to the Land, and terminated in a Nook. It is a kind of Lesser Gulph, bigger than a Creek, and Is BE A B E A larger in the Middle within, than ’ ris at the En - trance into it; which Entrance is called the Mouth of the Bay.

beacons.c: BEACONS, are Fires maintained on the Sea - coafts, to prevent Ship - wracks, and to give notice of Invafions, &c.

beadle.c: BEADLE ( in Law ) signifies a Messenger or an Apparitor of a Court, that cites Men to the Court to appear and answer.

beakorbeak.c: BEAK, or Beak - head, of a Ship, is that Part of it which is fattened to the Stem, and is supported by a Kyiee and is the becoming Part or Grace of a Ship.

beamcompasses.c: BEAM COMPASSES, is an Instrument made in Wood or Brass, with Hiding Sockets to carry several fliifting Points, in order to draw Circles with very long Radii: They are of good use in large Projections for drawing the Furniture on Wall Dyals, tie.

beams.c: BEAMS of a Ship, are the great main crois Tim - bers which hold the Sides of a Ship from falling together, and which also support the Decks and Orlops. The Main Beam is next the Main Matt, and from it they are reckoned by First, Second, or Third Beam. The great Beam of all is called tfie Midjkip Beam.

bearaword.c: BEAR, a Word used by Seamen in several Sen - fes. They fay a Ship Bears Ordnance, when fire Carries any great Guns: She Bears a good Sail, they fay, when a Ship having ’ her Sails abroad in a Gale of Wind, fails upright in the Water. When a Ship fails toward the Shore, she is said to bear in with the Land: When a Ship that was to Wind - ward comes under another Ship ’ s Stern, and so gives her the Wind, she is said to Bear under her Lee. If a Ship fails into an Habour with the Wind large, or before the Wind, she is then said to Bear in with the Harbour and when a Ship keeps off from any Land, she is said to Bear off from it. When a Seaman would express how any Cape or Place lieth from another, he faith it beareth off so, or so. In Conding also, they fay, Bear up the Helm, i. e. let the Ship go more large before the Wind; and Bear up Bound, that is, let tbe Ship go between her two Sheats, directly before the Wind. Lastly, There is another Sense of this Word in reference to the Burthen of a Ship ( which Word is derived from hence ) for they fay a Ship Bears, when having too slender or Lean a Quarter slie will sink too deep into the Water, with an o - ver - light Freight, and thereby can carry but a small Quantity of Goods.

bear.c: BEAR, is also used in Heraldry: He that hath a Coat of Arms is said to Bear in it the several Charges or Ordinaries that are in his Escutcheon; as if there are Lions Rampant in it, he is said to Bear Lions Rampant.

BEAR; there are two Constellations of the Stars called by this Name, the Greater and Lesser Bear, or ' Orfa Major and Minor. The Pole Star is said to be in the Tail of the Letter, because that Star is never above Degrees distant from the N. Pole of the World.

bearinginnavigation.c: BEARING, in Navigation, signifies the Point of the Compass that one Place bears or stands off from another.

bechicks.c: BECHICKS, are Medicines good against Cough. They are called also Bechkal Medicines t Blanchard. ’ M bed; / B EZ

bed.c: BED, of the Carriage of a Great Gun, is that thick Plank which lies immediately under the Piece, being as it were the Body of the Carriage.

belandre.c: BELANDRE, is a fort of little Vessel with Sai ’ s and Tackle like an Hoy, but Broader and Flatter: The covering of the Deck is raised up half a Foot higher then the Gunwale, Gunnel, or Plat - board, as the French call stand between the Gunnel and the Deck there is a Passage left free, for the Seamen to walk upon: They ate chiefly ufedtocarry Merchants Goods, and are seldom above Tun. Some will have them called By - flanders, because they seldom go out of fight of, but fail by the Land,

belay.c: BELAY, aboard a Ship, signifies the fame as Fallen: Thus they fay belay the Sheat, or Tack., that is, fasten it to the Kynnel, &c.

belenoides.c: BELENOIDES, is the process or Ihooting forth of the Bone called Aliformis, vhich is fixed in the Basis of the Skull. Blanchard. SELLANDER: SzeBclandrc.

bend.c: BEND; at Sea they fay Bend the Cable, when tis to be seized and made fast to the Ring of the Anchor; and to Bend tvto Cables, is all one with them as to tye them together. To unbend the Cable is toloofen it from the Ring of the Anchor, which is done when a Ship designs to be long at Sea. To bend a Main - Saile, is to make it fast to the Yard in its proper place.

BEND, one of the Eight Honourable Ordinaries inHeraldry, containing a fifth when uncharged, but when charged, a third part of the Escutcheon. It ’ s made by twoLines drawn thwart - ways from the Dexter Chief to the Sinister Base Point; thus. He bear - eth Or, a Bend Sable; A Bend is subdivided into a

bendlet.c: BENDLET, which is the sixth part of the Shield; a Garter, which is the Moiety of a Bend; a Coss, which is the th part ofa Bend; and a Bfbbo which Is the Moiety of a Cost. There is alio a Bend Sinijler, which is drawn from the Sinijler chief Point to the Dexter base, and this is subdivided into the Scrape or Scarp, and the Battoonei which latter is the th part of the Bend. This Battoone is the most usual Mark of Ille - gitimacy, but then it never extends it self quite athwart the Shield, but is cut off a little at each End. When two streight Lines drawn within the Bend run nearly parallel to the outward Edges of it, that is called Voiding, and he that bears it is laid to bear a Bend voided thus He beareth Ermine, a Bend void - Gules.

bendytheterminblazonary.c: BENDY, the Term in Blazonary for an Efcut - pheons being divided Bendways into an eyewNum - ber of Partitions; but if they are odd the Field must first be named, and then the Number of the Bends.

benigndiseases.c: BENIGN Diseases, are those which are not at - tended with anomalous, and extremely violent Symptoms.

bermeinfortification.c: BERME, in Fortification, is a ' little Space of Ground three, four, or five Eoot wide, left without, between the Foot of the Rampart and the side of the Moat, to receive the Earth that rolls down from thence, and to prevent its falling into the Moat. Sometimes for more Security the Berme Is Pallifa - dose

berkingaship.c: BER KING a Ship, by some is ment the as - sing up of the Ship's Sides.

besayle.c: BESAYLE ( in J. aw ) is a Writ that lies for the Heir, where his Great Grand - father was seized the Day that he died, or died seized of Land in Fee - simple and stranger enters theDay of theDeath of the Great Grand - Father, or abates after his Death,, his Heir shall have a Writ against such a Diffeifor or Abater.

bevelaninstrument.c: BEVEL, an Instrument well known to Builders, ’ Carpenters, and Bricklayers, and used for adjusting of Angles.

bevileaterminheraldry.c: BEVILE, a Term in Heraldry, signifying Broken, or opening like a Carpenter's Rule. Thus he beareth Argent a chief Bevile vert. by the Name fBeverlis.

bewpleader.c: BEWPLEADER, is a Writ that lies where the Sheriff, or other Baliff in his Court will take & Fine of the Party, Plaintiff or Defendant, to the end that he shall not plead fairly, c.

bezantsorbefants.c: BEZANTS or Befants, a Term in Heareldry sot Round Plates of Gold without any Stamp, which, are born frequently in Coats of Arms: GuiUim says, a Beafant or Beafaunt is taken for a Massy - Plate of Gold of lb. and Ounces weight; though some think they were smaller Pieces stamp at Byzantium or Gonjlantinople; whence the Name.

bezoaranimate.c: BEZOAR Animate, according to some, is the Liver and Heart of Vipers dried and powdered.

bezoarminerale.c: BEZOAR Minerale, is an Evaporation of the Solution of Butter of Antimony in Spirit of Nitre, ’ till white Mass remain at the bottom: On this new Spirit of Nitre is poured, and the Liquor eva - ported again; and this is a third time repeated then the Matter is Calcin ’ d for about half an Hour, which will turn it into a white Powder fit for use. Mr. Boyle calls it Be oardicum Minerale.

bezoardigumorbe.c: BEZOARDIGUM or Be artick. Remedies, of Cordial, are filch as arc endued with a Vertue to resell and expel Poison and Malignity.

bezoardigum.c: BEZOARDIGUM jovial, is a Bygule made by; melting Ounces of Regule of Antimony with i Ounces of Block - Tin, which being powdered is mix - ed with Ounces of Sublimate Corrosive, and then is distilled off in a kind of Butter; which Butter is afterwards dissolved in Spirit of Nitre ( of thrice its weight, ) and then the Solution is distill ’ d three times. The Be oar will remain at the bottom; which must be powdered, and wash, and then mingled with Spirit of Wine, and digested till it growinfipid.

bezoardicumlunale.c: BEZOARDICUM Lunale, is made by mixing Ounces of Redtify ’ d Butter of antimony, with an Ounce of fine silver, a dthendifloived inSpirit ofNitre, which must be poured on gently fresh and fresh till alPthe Ebullitions are over, then the Spirit is drawn off from the Matter with a gentle Heat ( with three Rectifications ) and then the Be oar is managed like the Jovial Be oar: Which fee.

bezoardicummarti.c: BEZOARDICUM Marti ale, is a Dissolution of Crocus Martis made by Reverberation ( or at least as much of it as can be effected ) in Butter of An - simony; and then Spirit or Nitre is poured on it, and they proceed as in the other Be oardick, Pre - parations.

biceps.c: BICEPS, is a Muscle of the Cubit, io called be - use it hath two Heads or Beginnings; the first, or outraoft, arises with a long round Tendon from the upper part of the Brink of the Acetabulum Sca - pulae, and runs tinder the Ligament of the Articu - lation in a Sulcus or Channel on the Head of the Shoulder - bone, where it is inclosed by a proper Ligament. In its descent it begins to grow fleshy as it marcheth tinder the Termination of the Pediorral Muscle, where dilating it self into a large fleshy Body, in joyns with its other Head or Beginning. The latter ariseth with a somewhat board, flat and long Tendon at the extremity of th tProceJfus Cara - eoides Scapula: in its descent ’ it strictly adheres to the Corqcobrachialis, ( wherefore some Authors not rightly describing that Muscle amongst thole of the Arm, have mistaken it for a fleshy beginning of ihis ) But then parting from it, both these Heads compose a large fleshy Belly, which becoming Tendinous neat the Cubit, is commonly said to be infertedby a strong round Tendon to the Tubercle at the upper Head of the Radius. But we ( ' says Cowper ) have observed this Tendon to be double the External of which being thin, passeth oblique - ly over the Musculus Pronator Radii Teres, and Membrane - like expanding it self, joins with the Membrana Communis Mufculorum, which embraceth all the External Muscles of the Carpus and Fingers: when this Muscle dieth the Cubit is bended.

bicepsamuscle.c: BICEPS, a Muscle of the Leg, called sometimes biceps Femoris, to distinguish it from the Biceps Cubiti. It hath two Heads, the superior and long - eft of which arileth with a round Tendon from the from the Protuberance of the Ischium - in its descent it becomes large and fleshy, and in above half itsPro - grefs lessens it self again, where it is joined with its other Head, having a broad, partly Tendinous and partly Fleshy beginning from the Linea Afipera of the Os Femoris, immediately below the Termina - tion of the Gluttons Maximus it being thus united, grows Tendinous, as it marcheth in a Channel on the External Appendix of the Os Femoirs, becoming perfectly Tendinous at its Ini plantation to the Su - periour Epiphysis of the Fibula Its use is to help bend the Tibia; it is likewise employed in turning the Leg, together with the Foot and Toes, outwards, when we fit with the Knees bended.

bigamy.c: BIGAMY, signifies, either, as formerly, those that were married more than once, which was then an Impediment that hindered a Man from be - ing a Clerk or as used in Common - Law, to have mote than one Wife at the fame time;

bightorbite.c: BIGHT or Bite, is any turn or part of a Rope that lies compassing and therefore when they can - not take the End of a Rope in Hand the Seamen fay, give me a Bite.

bilanciisdeferendis.c: BILANCIIS Deferendis, is a Writ directed to a Corporation, for the carrying of Weights to such a Haven, there to weigh the Wools that such a Man is Licensed to Tranlport.

bildge.c: BILDGE, of a Ship, is the Bottom of her Floor, Bildge Water therefore is that which by reason of the Flatness of a Ship ’ s Bottom lies on her Floor, and cannot go to the Well of the Pump; and con - sequently the Dutch, whose Ships are often of this Form, do much use a fort of Pumps called Bildge Pumps, or as we call them. Burr - Pumps, to carry off this Bildge Water: Also when a Ship strikes on a Rock, they fay, She is Bildged, And Bill age is the Breadth of her Floor when Hie lies ground.

bile.c: BILE, or the Gall, is a Liquor partly Sulphur - reous, and partly Saline, which is separated from the Blood of Animals in the ( Liver for the re - ceiling and evacuating of which there have been reckoned only two Vessels or Passages, that is, the Gall Bladder and the Porus Bilarius. By this latter there flows a thicker but miller by the former a Thinner, and more Acrimonious and Fer - tentative Choler into the Intestine, But besides these, there have been lately found out a Thirds which we shall describe by and by. The Gall - bladder, called inGreek masts ' go vFbrtoj in Latin Vesica bilkria, or Folliculus fellis, is a hol - low Bag placed in the under or hollow Side of the Liver, and in Figure reprefenteth a Pear. It is a - bout two Inches in length, and one in breadth, where broad eft. By its upper Part it adheres to the Liver, ' which doth afford it a Holjownefs to lodge in. j but the lower Part, which hangeth without the Liver, resteth upon the Right Side of the Stomach and the Colon, and doth often dye them both Yellow. It hath three Membranes, one common, which is thin and outmost. This springing from the Mem - brane of the Liver, only covereth that Parc which hangeth without the Liver. The two other Mem - branes are proper. The Middle is thick and strong and muscular, and hath three Ranks of Fibres the outer most are transverse, the middle oblique and the innermost streight. But some will allow only two Ranks, vi. the Streight, which run lengthways of it, and are outer; and the Trans verse or Annular, which are the inner. The inmost Coat is Nervous, or Tendinous as k were and to the Inside of this there adhereth a kind of Glandulous Coat. The Glands herein do separate from the Arteries a kind of Mucous Hu - mour, which fervesto defend the Vesica from being irritated by the Acrimony of the Choler contained in it. “ W - ', there is a Third, betwixt that I called common and the middle, and says, it is so evident, that he wonders this quick - sighted Age has not yet discover ’ d it. It is interwoven with whitish Fi - bres drawn diversly and irregularly, and has a - bundanceof Nerves and Sanguiferous Vessels run - ning through it, whose chief Branches run mostly. from its Neck towards its Bottom and upon this ' Account this Coat may be termed Vascular. In fat People it contains much Fat, and With a'litde Labour is separated into divers Flakes ( or Plates. ) It hath two Parts, the Bottom and the Nec / g The Bottom is its larger or wider Part that con - tains the Choler, and is. of the fame Colour with the Bile that is in it whence it commonly looks Yellow, but sometimes Greenish, Blackish, The Neck otherwise called Meatus Cysticus ) is its narrower Part, being but about. as wide as a Goose - quill, and about two Inches lon Be - twixt this and the Vesica there is a certain Fibrous Ring, which much straitens the Passage and so hinders the two hasty Repletion of the Vesica The other End of the Neck is joined to the Porus Bila - nm, and they both make the DuHus Corhmunx or common Passage of the Choier, - which is inferred into the Beginning of the Jejunum, or the End of the Duodenum. I Ww has observed. that ia ms - M Z ny / ny Birds ?, and some Fifties, this Meatus does not join the Porus bilarius, but is inferred separately in - to the Guts. The Ancients ( whole Opinion is of late stilly defended by Dr. Cole ) thought that the Choier in the Gall - bladder was received in by its Neck from the Poms bi lari us, and that it passed out into the common Dudk the fame way. And to obviate the Objection, that there uses not to be a Reciproca - tion of Humours in the fame Vessel ( at the fame time especially. j Dr. Cole supposes, that the Gall passes out of the Gall - bladder only in the time of the distribution of the Chyle, but at all other times it is received into it from the Porus, and is stored tip in it against the next Occasion. Butnot to en - ter into this Dispute, I think Dr. Glijfons Account of it the more probable, which is this: The ord - nary way of filling the Gall - bladder, is by its Fi - brous Roots that are dispersed through the Liver. The whole Trunk of these Roots enters that Part of the Bladder where ’ tis strained by a Fibrous Ring. This Trunk indeed hardly equals the Hundredth Part of the Roots of the Porus Bilarius; yet it distributes some Twigs and Capillary Ves - self into the hollow Side of the Liver. But if you open the Gall - bladder with a Design to underhand the Manner of the Insertion of this Trunk into it, truly you will not easily find it. For though this Dudl do penetrate the said Bladder, and the Hu - mour contained in it be discharged thereinto; yet there is hardly any Print or Sign of this Hole in the Inside of the Bladder: Which ought not to seem hard to be believed by any one, if he remem - ber the Insertion of the Ureters into the Vesica; for though these do far exceed this Trunk in Width, yet one can hardly find their Insertion if he cut o -, pen the Bladder and look for it. The best way ( that I could yet find ) to discover the Infection of this Trunk ( if you will open the Gall - bladder, andfearch for its Entrance into it ) is thus; look carefully for a certain little and spongy Protube - rance near the Orifice of the Bladder hard by the Meatus - Cyjlicus for the aforesaid Trunk, I think, is pretty plainly inferred into that Protube - rance. This Protuberance is called a Valve by Shige - llas. Besides this Mr. Perault has found out another new Conduit for the Bile, which he calls Ductus csl - hepaticus, becaufeit is common both ' to the, Vcficulazx tl the Porus Hepaticus ( ov Bilarius ). This Dud: has three Roots, which being subdivided in - to numerous Twigs, are dispersed through the Pa - renchyma of the Liver, amongst the Branches of the Vena Cava and Porta: These Roots grow into one Trunk, which creeping along the Surface of the hollow Side of the Liver, has a double Im - plantation; one into the Porus Bilarius, two In - ches and an half before the said Porus ’ s, uniting with the Meatus Cy ficus; and another into the Middle of the Vesica ( on that Side of it which ad - heres to theLiver ) with a Valve. This Valve seems to be formed of the inner Membrane of the Vesica, and also a proper one, and may be said to be a kind of middle Valve, between the Nature of the Sigmoides and Triglottis ( or Trifcupis ) of the Vena Arteriosa and Arteria Venosa in the Heart. Be - twixt its Insertion intothe Porus Bilarius, and this into the Vesica, there is about fix Inches length. It contains a thinner Choier ip it than the Porus Bilarius Jo, Alph. Bcrellus ( Professor of the Mathema - ticks at Naples ) from the continual and Ipeedy Ef - flux of the Bile by the Dpclus Communis into the Duodenum, believes, that there is a particular Cir - cubation of it: For he affirms, That in a Day ’ s time, from a Person falling, there pass thirty four Pound of Bilious Juice into the Duodenum by the common DuEl, whereas the whole Mass of Gall is not two Pound: Whence he concludes, that so great a quantity of Gall cannot be produced in the Liver by way of Fermentation, but that it is sea ? rated Mechanically, without the help of any Fer - ment, only by Cibraticn, from the Minute Vessels of the Porta through the Pores of the Glandules of the Liver, as the Urine is separated in the Kid - neys; so he infers, that there is a particular Cir - cubation of the Bills through the Abdomen, per - formed by the Verne Mefaricce into the Trunk of the Porta, thence to the Liver, thence through the Bilious Vessels into the Duodenum, to return again by the Mefaraick Veins. He that would enquire more into this Novel, and ( to mej improbable O - pinion, may consult his Opus Pofthumum ( pars al - tera ) de motu Animalium. It has been taught by several Anatomists, That its Neck or Meatus has sometimes two, sometimes three Valves, to hinder the Recourse of the Choier; but Diemerbroecl i processes he could never find any but only that the Egress of the Vesica was very ) strait, and its Neck wrinkled. Dr. Gliffon de - clares also, That he has open ’ d very many Ves ' self of this kind, and never yetfaw a Valve in any; of them: But he thinks that the Fibrous Ring ( a - above - mention ’ d ) did impose upon those who have thought there was a Valve. Besides, upon tryal he has often found, that the Bile by a light Com - prefilonof the Fingers, has fluduated to and again out of the Cyfiis into the Meatus, and on the con - trary; as also out of the Meatus into the DuBm Communis and back again: " Winch certainly could not be, if there were any Valve in the way, for that would hinder the one or other of these Moti - ons; The Vesica Felt'ea hath two Veins called Cyfiicce Gemellce, which spring from the Porta. It hath Twigs of Arteries proceeding from the right Branch of the Cceliaca; and it hath a small thread - like Sprig of a Nerve from the Mefenterical Branch of the intercostal. Many times Stones are found in it, which are lighter and more upon gy than those of the Urinary. Bladder, and will swim above Water, which these latter will not do. The other Passage which carrieth the thicker fort of Choier, is called Porus Bilarius, or Meatus Hepaticus, because it passes directly from the Liver to the Ductus Communis. Within the Liver, its Trunk and Branches are invested with a double Coot; its proper one which it retains without the Liver also, and another that is common to it with the Porta, called Capsula Com - munis, which it has from the Membrane of the Liver. In this common Coat this Porus and the Porta are so closely enwrapped, that you would take them but for one Vessel, till you hold ir ei - ther up to the Light ( " which will discover Vessels of two " Colours in it ) or very dexteroufty rip up the Capsula, and so lay them open. Its Roots within the Liver are equally divided with those of the Porta every where, having that little Space where the Roots of the Vesica pit spread in the Sinuous / OIL OIL Sinuous and Right - side of the Liver. So that ha - ving spoken above of the Divisions of the Roots of the Porta, I flvall only observe, that they are far larger and more numerous than those of the Ve - Jica, drawing Choler from all the Parts of the Li - ver ( saving whither the Roots of the Bladder reach J and that more thick and viscous, yet less Acrimonious. This Porus seems to be a more necessary Part than the Vesica for many Creatures, as Harts, Fallow Deer, the Sea - Calf, &c. and those which have a whole Hoof, as an Horse, &c. have no Gall - Bladder, but there is none that is destitute of this. Without the Liver it is as wide again as the Meatus Cysticus, with which it is joined at two Inches distance from the Liver, and both make the Duftus Communis Choledochus. It has no Valve in its whole Progress; only the Bu & us Communis, where it enters the Intestine, ha - ving pierce ’ d the outer Coat, passes betwixt that and the Middlemost about the twelfth Part of an Inch, and at last opens with a round Mouth into the In - testing. So that this oblique Insertion ( as that of Ureter into the Urinary Bladder ) serves instead f a Valve to hinder any thing from regurgitating out out of the Gut into this Dudt, especially the inmost Tunicle of the Intestine hanging so flaggy before its Mouth, that when any thing would enter in, it claps close upon it and stops it. As to any uajiomofes of the Roots of any of these Biliary Vessels, with those of the Vena Porta iuch indeed have been much talk ’ d of, but without truth, for their extreme Twigs or Capillaries ter - minute in the Parenchyma of the Liver, out of whose Grape - stone - like Glandules they imbibe theGhoier there separated from the Blood - as is the Case of the Capillaries of the Cava, for they receive the Blood it self imported by the Porta, in like manner, without any Inosculations. The Vfe of all these Vessels may sufficiently be learned by what has already been said of them j though some are of Opinion, that not only Choler, but other fuperfiuous Humours are evacuated by them, especially upon taking a Purge. The Ancients look upon the Bile as a meer Ex - cement, or at least, to be of no other use than by its Acrimony to promote the Excretion of the Guts: Which Opinion continued as long as the Liver was thought to be the Vas Sangnificans. But when once that Viscus was discovered to have scarce any other Office, then to separate the Choler from the Blood, it hath seemed unreasonable to suppose so large a Bowel was made only for the separation of a meer Excrement; and therefore its now generally be - lieved, that the Bile is the proper Ferment for both the Chile and the Blood. A very good Account of the manner of which Diembroeck, gives us, as sol - lows: The Blood flowing into the Liver by the Porta, out of the Gaftrick and Mefaraick Veins ( and, it may be, a little by the Hepatick Artery ) is mixed with an Acrimonious, Saltish, and Subacid Juce ( made in the Spleen, of the Arterious Blood flowing thither by the Arteries, and of the Animal Spirits by the Nerves ) which is brought into the Porta by the Ramus Splenicus, Now both these being entred the Liver by the Branches of the Porta, by means of this said Acrimonious and Acid Juice, and the Specifick Verrue or Cocftion of the Liver, the Spi - rituous Particles, t oth Sulphureous and Salt, lying hid in the said Venous Blood, are dissolved, attenuate ' ed, and become alio a little Acrimonious and Fer - meeting a certain thinnest part whereof like most clear Water, being separated from the thicker Mass of Blood, by means of the conglomerated Glands placed mostly in the hollow Side of the Li - ver, is carried from thence by many Lymphedudts, as has been said. But the Fermentaceous Spirits of greater Acrimony, mixed with the thicker and morevilcid sulphureous Juices ( for Sulphur is vi - said ) and more strongly boiled, when as through the Clamminess of the Juices in which they inhere they cannot enter the conglobated Glands, nor from them the Lymphedudb, and yet through their fierce Ebullition are separated from the Blood ( as Yest from Beer ) these Fermentaceous Spirits, I fay, being fever ’ d with the Juice in which they in - here, become bitter, and are called Bile which Bile being transcolate through the Grape. stone like Glandules in the Roots of the Porus Bilarius P and of the Gall - bladder, passes through them by the DuHus Communis into the Duodenum or Jeju - num, where itisprefently mixed with the Pan ere - atick Juice, and both of them with the Alimentary Mass, concocted in the Stomach, and now passing down this way, which it causes to ferment. And because at its first Entrance it is more Acrimonious ' and has its Vertue entire, and so causes the great - eft Ebullition with the Pancreatick Juice; hence the Milky Juice contained in the Mass conceded in the Stomach is more readily, and in greatest quantity separated in the Jejunum, and by insume - table Ladleal Vessels ( which are more numerous in this than the other Guts ) it is more quickly driven on towards the Receptdculum Chyli, and - this is the Reason that this Gut is always so empty. But in thrfollowing Guts, because the Fermentaceous Spirits ate a little pall d, the Effervefcency be - comes flower and less efficacious, and the Chyle is more slowly separated from the thicker Mass, and therefore they have sewer Vena Laelea. At length What remains of this fermenting Matter, is mixed with the thicker Faeces in the great Guts, where by its Acrimony it irritates them to Excretion.
