BY - LADDER, See Belandre. BY - LAWS, are Orders made in Court - Leets or Court - Barons by common consent, for the good of those that exa t them, and which extends farther than the Publick Law binds. Blunt.

bookii.c: BOOKII. Prof. I. The Phcenomena of Colours in reflected or re - fracted Light are not caused by new Modi - fications of the Light variously imprest, ac - cording to the various Terminations of the Light and Shadow. For by this th Experiment, Bool l. ’ tis evident that the Sun s Light being tranlmited into a dark Room through the parallel Surface of two Prisms fastned together in the Form of a Parallelopiped, became totally of one Colour ( either uniformly Yellow or Red ) ar its emerging out of the Prism: In the Production of which Colour the Confine of Shadows ( he Ihews ) can have nothing to do, be - cause the Light changes irom White to Yellow, Orange and Red successively, without any alter - tion of the Confine of Shadow: At both Edges of the emerging Light where the contrary Confines of Shadow ought to produce different Effects, the Colour is one and the fame, whether it be White, Yellow, Orange or Red j and in the Middle of the emerging Light where there is no Confine of Shadow afe all, the Colour is the very fame as at the Edges, the whole Light at its Entrance being of one uniform Colour, whether White, Yellow, Orange or Red, and going on thence perpetually without any change of Colour, such as the Confine of Shadow is vulgarly supposed to work in its re - fracted Light at its Emergence. Neither can thele Colours arise from any new Modifications of the Light by Refractions, be - cause they change successively from White to Yet - low, Orange or Red, while the Refractions re - main the fame; and also because the Refractions are made contrary ways by parallel Superficies which destroy one another ’ s Effects. He shews also in Experiment the First of this d Book, That by applying an Iron Wire, or such like Body, to a proper Part of a very large Prism, posited about Feet from the Hole of a darkened Room, you may so intercept the Rays at their Entrance, as to take away any one Colour ( which you please ) either wholly or in part, out of the Speftrum or coloured Image, and leave the reft re - maining; which shews that all Colours have an Indifference to any Confines of Shadow, and therefore the Differences of these one from ano - ther don ’ t arise from the different Confines of Shadow, whereby the Light is variously model ’ d, as hath hitherto been the Opinion of Philosophers. Again, a Lens being placed about Feet from the Prism at the Hole, had a Paper placed in its So - cus, which, when it was situate perpendicular to the Light, appeared of its own colour White, but when very much oblique appear ’ d Yellow and Red when inclined one way, and Blue when turn - ed another, and yet here the Confines of Light and Shadow, and the Refractions of the Prism remained in all Cafes the fame. And the Reason of the Phenomenon ( he shews ) is this, That the Paper in one Posture being more oblique to the more refrangible Rays than to the less, is more strongly illuminated by the latter than by the for - mer; and therefore the less refrangible Rays are predominant in the reflected Light, and wherever they are so, they tinge the Light with Yellow or Red j as when the Paper being placed in the con - trary way, and in an oblique Posture, the more re - frangible Rays become predominant; and they al - ways tinge the Light with Blues and Violet Co - lours. Prop. II. All Homogeneal Light hath its proper Colour answering to its degree of Refrangibility; and that Colour cannot bes changed by Reflecti - ons and Refractions. This is plain by Experiment, for after he had separated the several forts of Rays one from ano - ther ( as he shews how to do in th q Experiments be - longing to the th Propof. of his First Book, ) and by that means got a quantity of Homogeneal Light; this Spot of Homogeneal Light was afterwards un - capable of being changed by either Refraction or Reflection, and all Bodies placed in that Homoge - neal Light still appear ’ d of its Colour,, however different their own proper Colours were from that. From whence he concludes, That if the Suns Light confided but of one fort of Rays, there would be but one Colour in the whole World nor wofild it be possible to produce any new Colour by Re - flections and Refractions; andconfequently all the variety of Colours depend upon the Composition of Light, Prop. III. Problem, To define the Refrangibility of the several forts of Homogeneal Light answering to the see - ral Colours. In this the Author is very curious and exact f hewing the Laws of the Refractions out of Glass into Air, whence by the Axioms of his First Book, the Laws of Refractions out of Air into Glass are easily derived. And finding by Experiment, that when Light goes out of Air thro ’ several contigu - ous refracting Mediums fas thro ’ Water and Glass ) and thence goes out again into Air, whether the refracting Surfaces be parallel or inclined to one another; that Light, as often as by contrary Re - fractions tis so corrected, as that it emergeth in Lines parallel to those in which it was incident continues ever after to be White i But if the ever - gent Rays be inclined to the incident, the white - ness of the emerging Light, will by degrees, in passing on from the place of Emergence, become tinged in its Edges with Colours. He thinks he can gather two Theorems ( which he there gives ) and by which the Refractions of the Rays of eve - ry fort, made our of any Medium into Air, are known by having the Refraction of the Rays of one fort; and also the Refraction out of one Me - dium into another, may be had as often as you have the Refractions out of them both into any third Medium. And these Theorems, if admitted into Opticks, would give a scope to treat that Subject voluminously after a new manner, not only by teaching those things which tend to the Perfection of Vision, but also by determining, Mathematical - ly, all kinds of Phenomena of Colours which could be produced by Refraction, Prop. IV. Colours may be produced by Composition, which shall be like the Colours of Homogeneal Light, as to the Appearance of Colour, but not as to the Immutability of it, and the Constitution of Light - and thole Colours, by how much more they are compounded, by so much are they less full and intense; and by too much Compoli - tion they may be diluted and weaken ’ d, till they cease. There may lib Colours be pro - duced by Composition, which are not fully like any of the Colours of Homogeneal Light, Prop. V. . Whiteness, and all Grey Colours between White and Black, may be compounded of other Co - lours; and the Whiteness of the Sun's Light is compounded of all the primary Colours mixed in a due Proportion. This he proves by many Experiments, and in particular by this; That a Lens being placed to receive the colour ’ d Speftrum cast from a Prism at the Hole of a darkened Room, [ the Light in the Focus of the Lens converged, and there made a bright Spot, which received on a white Paper there, and in a right or normal Position to the Rays, appeared White on the Paper; but if either the Paper be moved towards the Hole,, or behind the Focus of the Lens, it will presently begin to ap - pear coloured with the usual Colours of the Prism. Now the Reason of its appearing White at the So - cus, was, because there all the Rays were exactly mingled; for if any Colour, suppose the Fed or Blue, were by the Interpolition of some Body inter - cepted at the Lens; the Image in the Focus would never appear White, but some how coloured; so that to make Whiteness theBlending or Mixture of all the Rays is necessary. And then in Prop. VI. he proposes this Problem '. In a Mixture of primary Colours, the Quanti - ty and Quality of each being given, To know the Colour of the Compound. Prop. VIL All the Colours in the Universe which are made by Light, and depend not on the Power of I - imagination, are either the Colours of Homo - geneal Lights, or compounded of such; and that either accurately or very nearly, accord - ding to the Rule of the preceding Problem. For Book II. Prop. I. he shews, That the chan - ges of Colours made by Refractions, do not arise from any new Modifications of the Rays imprest by those RefraCtions, and by the various Termi - nations of Light and Shadow, as has been thecon - stant and general Opinion of Philosophers. He has likewise proved, that the several Colours of the Homogeneal Rays do constantly answer to their degrees of Refrangibility ( Prop. I. Lib. I. and Prop. II. Lib. II. ) and that their degrees of Refran - gibility cannot be changed by RefraCtions and Re - flections ( Prop. II. Lib. I. ) and by consequence, that those Colours are likewise immutable: He has also proved direCtly by refracting and reflect - ing Homogeneal Lights apart, that their Colours cannot be changed ( Pr. IL L. II. ) He has proved also, That when the leveral forts of Rays are mix ’ d, and in eroding pass through the fame Space, they do not a t so upon one another, so as to change each others colorifick Qualities ( Exp. X: L. IL ) but by mixing their Actions in the Sensorium beget [ a Sen fat ion differing from what either would do a - pare; that is, a Sensation of a mean Colour be - tween their proper Colours; and particularly, when by the Concourse and Mixtures of all forts of Rays a white Colour is produced, the White is a Mixture of all the Colours which the Rays would have apart ( Prop. V. Lib.. ) The Rays in that Mixture do not lose or alter their several Colori - sick Qualities, but by all their various kinds of A - ctions mix ’ d in the Sensorium, beget a Sensation of a middling Colour between all the Colours which is Whiteness; for Whiteness is a Mean be - tween all the Colours, having it self indifferently to all, so as with equal Facility robe tinged with any of them: ARedPowder mixed with a JittleBIue, i Blue with a little Red, doth not presently lose ts Colour; but a White Powder mixed with any Colour, is presently tinged with that Colour, and is equally capable of being tinged with any other Colour whatever: He has likewise shown, that as the Sun ’ s Light is mixed of all forts of Rays, so its Whiteness is mixture of the Colours of all forts of Rays; those Rays having from theBeginning their several colorifick Qualities, as well as their several Refrangibilities, and retaining them perpetually unchanged, notwithstanding any Refractions or Reflections they may at any time suffer, and that whenever any fort of the Sun ’ s Rays is by any, means ( as by Reflection in Exper. and. Lib. I. ) or by RefraCtion, as happens in all RefraCtions, separated from the reft, then they manifest their proper Colours. These things having been proved, says he, the Sum of all this amounts to the Proportion here to be proved; for if the Sun ’ s Light is mixed of fe - veral forts of Rays, each of which have originally, their several Refrangibilities and colorifick Quali - ties, and notwithftandingrtheir RefraCtions and Re - flections, and their various Separations and Mix - tures, keep those their original Properties perpetu - ally the fame without alteration; then all the Co - lours in the World must be such as constantly ought to arise from the original colorifick Qualities of the Rays, whereof the Lights consist by which those Colours are seen: And therefore, if the Reason of any Colour whatever be required, we have nothing else to do but to confider how the Rays in the Sun ’ s Light have by Refleions, or RefraCtions, or other Causes been parted from one another, or mixed together; or otherwise, to find out what forts of Rays are in the Light by which that Co - lour is made, and in what Proportion; and then, by thelaft Problem, to learn the Colour which ought to arise by mixing those Rays ( or their Colours; in that Proportion. After this in s Prop. VIII. and IX. He shews, how by these discovered Properties of Light, to explain the Colours made by Prisms, and also those of the Rain - bow. And then in . Prop. X. By the fame discovered Properties of Light, he explains the Permanent Colours of Natural Bodies. Shewing that their Colours arise from hence, that feme Natural Bodies refleCt some fort of Rays, and others other forts, more copiously and strongly than the reft: As for instance, Minium, Or Red - lead, reflects the least Refrangible, or Red making Rays, most copiously, and thence appears Red. Bat Violets rested the most Refrangible most copiously, and thence have their proper Colour; and so of other Bodies. Every Body refleds the Rays of its own Colour more copiously than the reft, and from their Excess and Predominance in the rested - ed Light, hath its Colour. TT, Then in his Second Boo k, Part I. and II. he takes into Consideration the Phenomena of those Colours which are ob'ferved in thin transparent Bodies, making many excellent ' Observations a - bout their Refledions and Refradions, and disc - vering many things as wonderful as they are cer - tain. And here he finds new reason to conclude, that the colorifiek Dispositions of Rays are also connate with them and immutable; and conse - quently, that all the Produdions and Appearances of Colours in the World are derived not from any Physical Change caused in Light by Refraction or Refledion, but only from the various Mixtures or Separations of Rays, by vertue of their different Refrangibility or Reflexibility; and in this helped the Science of Colours becomes a Speculation as truly Mathematical as any other part of Op ticks; that is, as far as they depend on the Nature of Light, and are not Creatures of the Imagination only. And in Part the Third, he discourse again of the permanent Colours of Natural Bodies, and thews the Analogy between them and the Colours of thin transparent Plates; as also shewing their Constitutions, whereby they rested some Rays more copiously than others: As also about the Colours which arise from the Infledion of the Rays of Light: In all which there is intermixed many ex - cellent Observations and curious Experiments re - latin to this most copious Subject See more un - der Light and Colour, in Vol. II. Prcmifcuous Observations and Experiments about Colours. It ’ s observable, that most transparent Bodies when they are either split, divided, or extended so that they have no sensible thickness upon their Surfaces, exhibit various Colours like those of the Rainbow. Thus is it with Muscovy Glass when split into exceeding thin pieces, and fine Glass when blown at the Flame of a Lamp into Bubbles as thin or thinner than the finest Paper; and so we lee it is in those Bubbles which Children make out of a mixture of Soap and Water, and those which arise from the shaking of almost any Chy - mical Oyl, or Spirit of Wine into very fine Froth: Mr. Boyle found that one Grain f Cochineal dissolved first into a pretty quantity of Spirit of U - rine, and then that Dissolution diluted with Wa - ter, would impart a sensible, though but a faint Colour, tofixGlaffes of Water, each of which contained Ounces and f, which amounts to a above times its own weight: And this shews the very great Divisibility of the Parts of Matter, as well as the Intestine Motion of the Parts of Fluid Bodies. The Ways by which a Liquor may suddenly change the Colour of another Liquor, or of ano - ther Body, Mr. Boyle thinks reducible to such as these. . By the Minute Particles of the Adventitious Liquors insinuating themselves into the Pores of the other, and filling them up either perse & ly or in part; by which means the Light passing through, the Liquor will be differently refracted from what it was before, when the Pores of it were only filled with Air, or perhaps some more subtile Fluid. . A Liquor may alter the Colour of a Body, by freeing it from those things which hindred it before from appearing in its genuine and proper Colour; as when Water ashes off the Filth of ordinary Bodies, and other Lixiviums or Menstruums clear away, or scour off the discolored Rust of Me - tals, &c. . By making a Comminution of the Parts of any Body, and that either by really subdividing them and making them less, or else by disjoining and separating such Aggregates or Clusters of Par - titles which clung together before. . Contrary to the last Way, the Colour of a Body may be changed by means of a Liquors ma - king Coalitions or Aggregates of several Particles, which before lay too scattered and dispersed to exhibit any Colour; and this way the new Co - lours of Precipitates may be supposed in part to arise. . A Liquor may also change the Colour of a Body, by dislocating and changing the Site and Po - sition of the Parts of it: Thus bruised Fruits ap - pear of a different Colour from their Ripe and Natural ones; and several Bodies are of a different Colour when dissolved in a Menstruum from what they had before. . The chiefeft and most important way of all, as being that which doth contain many others within it, is by associating the Saline Corpuscles or any other fort of the more rigid ones of the Liquor with the Particles of the Body that it is employed to work upon, and by that means must needs alter the Figure, Position, Bigness and de - gree of Motion of the Component Particles of that Body. banneret.c: BANNERET, was Anciently a Knight made in the Field with the Ceremony of cutting off the Point of his Standard, and making it as it were a Banner. And this was accounted so Honourable a Knighthood, that they were allowed to display their Arms in the Field in the King ’ s Preience as Barons do. They were next to Barons in Dignity. barometerportable.c: BAROMETER Portable, is one that can be safely and conveniently carried about from Place to Place, without the Danger of spilling the Mer - cury out of the Cistern, or letting the Air get in at the Bottom of the Tube, or of the Mercury in - clouded in the Tube breaking the Top of it off by the Motion it will be put into by being carried from one Place to another. You may prevent the two former Inconveniencies by tying some gentle Leather fast over the Brim of the Cistern, which ffiuft be of Glass or close grained Wood; and muff have a Jeck or Hollow round the outside of the Brim to tie on the Cover of Leather. And the Lift may be remedied, by either a way rd lere or squeeze the included Mercury quite up to the Top of the Tube, so that the Tube in its Carriage from Place to Place shall be always full; or else by winching the Head pf the Tube at about an Inch from the Top, so as to make it there have a very narrow Neck, not so big as a Straw: By which Means the Force of the Mercury striking against the Top, will be very much bridled, and ther & r fore the Tube secured from having its Top broken off.

A Bead is often placed on the lining Board of a Door - Case, and on the upper Edges of skirting Boards.

beam.c: BEAM,, in any Building, is a Piece of Timber lying across it, and into which the Feet of the prin - cial Rafters are framed. No Building hath less than two of these Beams, vi. one at each Head; and into these Beams the Girders of the Garret Floor are framed and if it be a Timber Build - ing, into them the Teazle Tendons of the Polls are also framed. These Teazle Tendons Hand at Right - angles to those which are made on the Polls to go into the Raifons, and the Relijh or Cheats of these Teazle Tendons Hand up within an t i Inch of the Top of theRaifon; and then the Beam is caused down ( which is all one as Dove - tailing across ) till the Cheeks of the Mortices in the Beam con - join with those of the Teazle Tendon on the Polls.

bearerinarchitecture.c: BEARER, in Architecture, is a Poll or brick Wall, which is trimmed up between the two Ends of a Piece ol Timber to Jhorten its bearing, or to prevent its bearing with the whole Weight at the Ends only.

beaupleader.c: BEAUPLEADER is, in Common Law, a Writ upon the Statute of Malridge lor not fair Plead - ing; and this lies where the Sheriff, or other Bay - lift in his Court, will take a Fine of the Party, Plaintiff, or Defendant, for that he pleaded not fairly.

bedmouldinginarchitedlure.c: BEDMOULDING, in Architedlure, is a Term used by the Workmen for those Members in a Cornilh which are placed below the Coronet or Crown; and now - adays a Bedmoulding usually conlills ol these Members, i. an O - G.. a Lift,. a large Boultine, and thlv, under the Co - rones another Lift.,

bedropbedrepe.c: BEDROP, Bedrepe, was the Customary Service which inferior Tenants formerly paid to their Lords, in cutting down their Corn, or doing any other. Work or Labour in the Field.

bends.c: BENDS, in a Ship, are the fame with the Wailes or Wales, which are the outmost Timbers of a Ship on which the Men let their Feet in climbing up: They are reckoned from the Water the first, second, and third Bend or Wail. They help much to ftreng - then the Ship, and have the Beams Knees and Foot - hooks bolted into them.

beneaped.c: BENEAPED: They fay at Sea a Ship is beep - ed, when it being a Nepe - Tide, the Water doth not flow high enough to bring her off from the Ground, out of the Dock, over the Bar, &c.

benefices.c: BENEFICES. All Church Preferments, ex - cept Bilhopricksj are by some called Benefices: Vid. Godolph. c. t h. And all Benefices are by the. Canonifts fomedmes called Dignities. But we now apply the Word Dignity to Bilhopricks, Dea - neries and Archdeaconries, and as some will have it to Prebends.

BENEFICES t e either Parfonages, Vicarages, or Donatives. Parfonages, are Churches endowed with Glebe, Manse, Tythes, and ail ether Ditties payable by the Parilhioners. Vicarages, ale Benefices which were cheated for the Maintenance of such Clergymen as served in Churches where some or all the Tythes were im - propriated. At first the Vicar was a meer Curate, but by Degrees some of them got a settled Mainte - ance distinct from the Impropriator, which confi - ned of a Manse and Glebe, and some Portions of Tythes usually; but in some Places only pension from the Impropriator. And these are what the Law calls Perpetu. d Vicars, or Vicars endowed. Donatives, are such as being exempt from the Jurisdiction of the Ordinary, are visitable only of the King or other Secular Patron, who puts his Clerk into Possession of the Benefice by virtue by an Instrument under Hand and Seal, without any Institution or Induction, and without any Examina - tion by the Ordinary. But the Clerk is obliged to subscribe the Declarations, and to take the Oaths enjoined by. c.. and. W. and M. the former before the Bishop in whose Diocese the Donative lies, and the latter before the Patron, faith Watfon. And if it be a Benefice with Cure, he is also bound to subscribe the Articles before the Bishop, to read the Common Prayer, and to make the fame Declarations as other Incumbents do,

beneficio.c: BENEFICIO ' prime Ecclejidllico halendo, is a Writ directed from the Queen to the Chancellour or Lord Keeper to bestow the Benefit that first shall fall in the Queens Gift, above or under such a Va - lue, on this or that particular Man.

benevolence.c: BENEVOLENCE is used both in our Statutes and Chronicles, for a voluntary Gratuity given by. the Subjects to the Sovereign.

besantine.c: BESANTINE was a Piece of Money coined by the Western Emperors at Byzantium or Cenftanti - noble, and was of two forts, Gold, and Silver, for - merly both current in England: The Silver Befan - tine was the Value of two Shillings, and the Gold was - v B I R BIS was of the Weight of a Ducket, as Chaucer fee ms to represent. benefigiumdivifionis.c: BENEFIGIUM Divifionis, in the Civil Law, is a Right by which the Creditor hall be forced, by way of Exception, to sue each Surety for their Share and Proportion, especially when the reft of the Sureties are under the Jurisdiction of the fame judge, and able to pay,

beneficium.c: BENEFICIUM Or dints five Excujfionis, in the Civil Law, is a Right by which the Surety can by way of Exception force the Creditor to sue the principal Debtor, before he half recover against him as the Surety, except the Surety was given ju - dicially in a Cause depending.

birds.c: BIRDS, are either Land - fowl or Water - fowl: Of Land fowl, some have crooked Beaks and Talons; and of these some are Carnivorous and Rapacious, being call ’ d Birds of Prey; some Frugivorous, and theie are called by the general Name of Parrots. Of Birds of Prey some are Diurnal, preying in the Day time; and of these they reckon a greater and lesser fort: The Greater are either of a more bold and generous Nature, as the Ea ? Je kind; or of a more cowardly and fluggifti, as the Vulture. - The Lesser Diurnal Birds of Prey in Latin are called Acc fines, the Hawk, kind; and these are either of a more bold and generous Nature, and are wont to be reclaimed and manned for fowling, and are called Hawk ? which our Falconers distinguish into Long - winged, as the Falcon, Lanner, ( c. whose Wings reach almost as far as the End of their Train; and short - winged, as the Goshawk and Spar - row Hawk, whose Wings, when closed, fall much - short of the End of their Trains. Those of the Hawk kind which are of a Nature more cowardly and fluggifti, or else indocible, are negleCted by our Falconers, and so live at large j and of these also there is a greater fort, as the Buggard kind; and a lesser, as the Butcher - bird or Shrike ( about as big as a Black - bird, and found in England ), The Bird. cf Paradise, which is exotick. Of Birds of Prey with crooked Beak and Ta - lons, some are NoBurnal, as the Owl kind, which fly and prey by Night; and these are either horned or eared, as the Eagle - Owl and Horn - Owl, ( c. or without Horns, as the Brown Owl, Grey Owl, ( c. There is a fort of Land Birds with crooked Beak and Talons which is called Frugivorous, be - cause though they do sometimes eat Flefli, and so are of the Carnivorous and Rapacious kind, yet they eat Fruits too; and these are known by the general Name of Parrots, and are distinguished in - to three forts according to their Bigness, the great - eft Size being called Maccaws; the middle sized, and most common, Parrots and Popinjays; and the least fort Parrakects; and all this kind make use of their Beak in climbing, and move the upper jaw. Land Birds that have their Bill and Claws more strait, are diftinguiftied into three Sizes. The great eft kind are such as by reason of the Bulk of their Bodies and Smallness of their Wings cannot fly at all; these are Exotick Birds of a Angular Nature, such as the Ostrich, the Cassowary, and the Dodo. The middle ft ( d kind are divided by their gills into such as have large, thick, strong, and Vol. II. long ones; some of which feed promiscuously on Flesh, Iniedts, and Fruits, as the Crow kind, which are wholly black; and the Pie kind, which are party coloured: Some feed on ( Filhonly, as the Kings - ff her - and some on Insects only, as the. Wood - pecker. And into such as have a ( sailer and a ( shorter Bill; whose Flesh is either white, as the Poultry kind; or blackish, as the Pigeon and Thrujh kind. The least figed kind of Land Birds with straight Bills and Claws, ar called small Birds; and these are of two kinds, vi. f oft beaked, which have lender, straight, and pretty longifti Bills most of them, and feed chiefly upon Insects; or hard beaked, which have thick and hard Bills, and feed mostly on Seeds. Water - fowl, are either such as frequent Water and watry Places to seek their Food; and these are all cloven footed, and generally have long Legs, and those naked or bare of Feathers for a good way a - above the Knees, that they may the more convent - ently wade in Waters. Of these they reckon two kinds a Greater, as the Crane, Jabiru, ( c. and a Les - fer which are either Piscivorous, Feeding on Fifth, as the Heron, Spoon - bill, Stork, ( c. or Mudfuckers and InfeBivorous: Of which some have very long Bills, which are sometimes crooked, as in the Curlew and Wbimbrell; and sometimes straight, as in the Wood cock and Godwitt. Others have middle jis Bills, as the Sea - pie and Red - shank, ( c. and a third fore have short Bills, as the Lapwing and Plover. Those are reckoned short Bills which exceed not an Inch and; middle sl ’ d are between x Inches p and if -; and long Bills above x Inches. There is another kind of Water - fowl which swim in the Water; some of which, as the Moor - hen and Coot, ( c. are cloven footed, but most are whole footed: And of these some few have very long Legs, as the Flammant, the Avofetta, and Corrira, ( lee Willoughby, Pan i... ) but mostly they are short legd: Of which some few have but three Toes on each Foot, as the Penguin, Ragor - bill, ( c. but generally they have four Toes on each Foot; and these either all connected together by intervene - ing Membranes, as in the Pelican, Soland Goose, ( c. or more usually with the back Toe loose And this kind are either narrow bill ’ d or broad bill'd; those with narrow Bills have them either blunt and hooked at the Tip, of which fort some are serrate, as in the Diver - kind, and some not toothed, as in the Puffin; or Sharp pointed and straighten, of which fort some have long Wings, as the Gull kind; and some Shorter, as those diving Birds called Douckers. Those with broad Bids may be divided into the Goose kind, which are larger, and the Duck kind which arefmaller; and these latter into Sea Ducks, or River and Plajh Ducks. Most Water - fowls have a short Tail; and none of this kincFhave their Feet disposed like Parrots and Woodpeckers, that have two Toes forward and two backward, none having more than one back Toe, and some none at all.

bindingjoyds.c: BINDING Joyds, in Architecture, are those Joyfts in any Floor into which the Trimmers of the Stair - Cafes and Chimney Waies are fram - ed; and these should be stronger than common Joyfts.

bishop.c: BISHOP. The whole Process of the Creation of a Biftiop, according to the Englijh Law, is thus: On the Vacancy of any See the Dean and Chapter are to certify the Queen thereof in Chancery, and to request her Leave to choose another Biftiop.. The Queen, when he pleases, fends her Conge ds E Eft ire B L A BOR EJUre, or Leave to elect, to the Dean and Chapter, ! nominating the Person whom sne thinks fit to have chosen. The Dean and Chapter are obliged with - in Days after the Receipt of this Conge dc EJUre to make the Election j which being accept - ted by the Person eledred, is certified both to the Queen and the Archbifliop of the Province. On this the Queen grants her Royal Assent under the Great Sea !, directed to the Archbifliop, together with a Mandate to Confirm and Consecrate him. The Archbishop gives a Commission to his Vicar General to proceed to Confirmation, which is a long formal Process, of which the most observable Parts are two, vi, a Citation of all such as have any Objections against the Bisliop EleCt, to appear before them and offer them, and then a DiduCti - on of all that has past in relation to the EleCtion and the Royal Assent; the Particulars whereof are exhibited by the ProCtor of the Dean and Chapter to the Vicar General. After this the Oaths of Su - primacy, Simony, and Canonical Obedience are taken by the Bisliop EleCt; on which Sentence is read, and subscribed by the Vicar General, where - by the EleClion is ratified and decreed to be good. Next to this follows the Consecration, which is performed by the Archbishop and two other Bi - slips: Then the Archbifliop fends a Mandate to his own Archdeacon to install the Bisliop in that Cathedral Church which belongs to his See, and this is ofreneft done by Proxy. And the publick Notary there present records the whole Process in an Authentick Instrument to be kept to Posterity j and after this the new Bishop is introduced to the Queen to. do Homage. On his Consecration the Bishop hath,. Right to his Temporakies, but he cannot sue for them till his Consecration be cert - fied by the Archbishop; but the Queen may grant the. ilioo his Temporakies immediately after his Confirmation. By his Confirmation he is inflated in the id ! diCtion of his Diocese, so as to excom - municate and certify it; and therefore the Power of the Guardian of the Spiritualties ceafesfrom that Tin forward. That for the Pro - suction of Black Colours, the Corpuscles must be left than any of those which exhibit other Colours, because at greater Sizes of the component Parti - cles, there is too much Light reflected to confti - tute this Colour j but if they be a little less, then is requisite to reflect the White and very faint Blew oftkefirft Ord r: Vid. They will reflect so little Light as to appear intense - ly Black and yet may perhaps reflect it variously to and fro within them so long, till it happen to be stilled and loft, by which means they will ap - pear. And from hence it appears why Fire, and that yet more subtle DifTolver PutrefaElion, by divi - ding the Particles of Subfiances, turn them Black.: Why small Quantities of black Substances impart their Colour very freely and intensely toothed Sub - stances to which they are applied the minute Particles of these, by reason of their very great Number,, easily over - spreading the grols Particles of others. Hence also it appears, why Glass ground very elaborately with Sand on a Copper - Plate, dll it be well polished, makes the Sand, to - gether with what by rubbing is worn off from the Glass and Copper, become very black: And why - black Substances do fooneft of all others become - hot in the Sun ’ s Light, and burn; ( which Eftecft may proceed partly from the Multitude of Refra - ctions in a little Room, and partly from the ealy Commotion of so very small Particles: ) And also why Blacks are usually a little inclined to a bluish Colour for that they are so, may be seen by illume - nating white Paper by Light reflected from black Substances, where the Paper will usually appear of a bluish White; and the Pveafon is, that black Borders on the obscure Blue of the first Order of Colours described in the above - mention ’ d th Ob - serration, and therefore reflects more Rays of that Colour than of any other. ’ Tis necessary also to the Production of Black ness in any Bodies that the Rays be stopt, retain ’ d, and loft in them; and these conceive Heat ( by means of a burning Glass, &c. ) more easily than other Bodies, because the Light which falls upon them is not reflected outwards, but enters the Bo - dies, and is often reflected and refraCted in them till it be stilled and loft.

braceinarchitecture.c: BRACE in Architecture, is a piece of Timber framed in with Bevil Joynts, and is used to keep the Building from swerving either Way: When a Brace is framed into the Kinglefles and principal Rafters, tis called by some a Strut.

bracketsingunnery.c: BRACKETS in Gunnery are the Cheeks of the Carriage of a Mortar: They are made of strong Planks of wood, of near a Semi - circular Form, and bound round with thick Iron Plates; they are fix ’ d to the Bed by Bolts, which are called Bed - bolts they rile up on each Side of the Mortar, and serve to keep her at any Elevation, by the Means of some strong Iron Bolts ( called Bracket - bolts ) which go through these Cheeks or Brackets.

brads.c: BRADS are Nails us ’ d in Building, having no spreading Heads as other Nails have: Of these some are called Joyners Brads, and are for hard Wainscot: others Batten Brads, and are for soft Wainfeot; and some Bill Brads or Quarter - heads, which are us ’ d when a Floor is laid in haft, or for hallow Joifts which are fubjeeft to warp.

brass.c: BRASS is a Metal made out of a Mixture of Cooper and Lapis Calaminaris ( which is usually called Calamine ). This Stone is dug out of several dines in the Weft of England ( as about Menditf, See. ) about Foot deep. It is burnt or calcined in an Oven or Kiln made red Hot, then ground to Powder, and sifted as fine as Flour; then mixt with ground Char - coal, because the Call - mine is apt to be clammy, to clod, and so is not easily incorporable. Then they put about of Calamine into a melting Pot, holding about a Gal - lon, and uppermost about ft of Copper. The Calamine must be mixt with as many Coals as will fill the Pot This is let down with Tongs into a Wind Furnace Foot deep, and remains there Hours - for they cast not off above twice in Hours / One Furnace holds Pots. After melting, B R I it is cast into Plates or Lumps. ft of Crude Calamine produces ft burnt or calcined. They use Brass Shruff some times instead of so much Copper; but that cannot always be procure ’ d in Quantities, being only a Collection of Pieces of old Brass. The best Brass Guns are made of malleable Metal, and cannot be made of pure Copper or Brass; but it is necessary to put in courser Metals to make it run dole and founder, such as Lead and Pot - metal. Bell - metal being Copper and Tin, and Pot - metal Copper and Lead. About ft of Lead is usually put into ft of Pot - Metal, but about ft is sufficient to put into a ft of Gun - me - tal. The Calamine Stones were heretofore fetch ’ d from Poland, but are now exported from us by the Dutch. The Manufacture of Brass was privately kept in Germany for many Hundreds of Years, wherein many Thousands were employ ’ d, and all were maintain ’ d, some having thereby rais ’ d themselves to great Estates. breastsinwomen.c: BREASTS, in Women and other Females, are of a Substance consisting of a great Number of oval Glands, lying in a great Quantity of Fat: Their Excretory DuCIs approach the Nipple, join and unite together, till at last they form seven, eight, or more small Pipes call ’ d Tubuli LaBiferi, which have seven cross Canals, by which they communicate with one another, that if any of them be stopt, the Milk which was brought to it might not stagnate, but pass through by the other Pipes, which all terminate in the Extremity of the Nipple. The Nipple is a Spongious Substance, made of two Orders of Fibres: The smallest make a fine Net - work within the largest spaces of the Net - work of the bigger Fibres. Through it pass the Tubuli LaBiferi, which grow smaller and smaller to their Extremities, that the Milk might not run out but when the Breasts are full, or upon Suction; It has an exquisite Sense, and a small Erection when it is handled. The Arteries and Veins of the Breasts are Branches of the Subclavian and Intercostal. They have Nerves from the Vertebral Pairs, and from the lixth Pair of the Brain. The Use of the Breasts is to separate the Milk for the Nourishment of the Foetus. The Arteries which terminate in the Glands, which compofethe Substance of the Breasts, bring the Blood pregnate ! with a Chyle which has received its last Perfection by its Circulation through the Lungs; this Chyle being separated by the Glands of the Breasts, runs through the Tubuli LaBiferi upon the SuCtion of the Child. The Breasts in Men are very small; they are chiefly for Ornament. I have seen some Men who have had Milk in them. Keih

brestsummers.c: BREST Summers, in a Timber Building, are the Pieces in the outward Parts of any Building, and in the middle Floors, ( not in the Garret, nor in the Ground Floor ) into which the Girders are framed.

bricks.c: BRICKS. The several kinds of Bricks used in Architecture arethefe: i. Comp of s Bricks, which are of a Circular Form, and are used in fteyning of Wells. z, Concave or hollow Briefs, being on one Side flat like a common Brick, but on the o - ther hollowed: They are used to convey Water. Cogging Bricks are used to make the indented Work under the Coping of Walls built of great Bricks.. Coping Bricks, which are formed on purpose for coping of Walls.. Dutch or Sse - rish Bricks, tiled to pave Yards and Stables, and for Soap - Boylers Salts, and for Citterns.. Clin - ksrs are such Bricks which are glared by the Heat of the Fire in the making.. Feather - edge Bricks arc like the common Statute Bricks, only they are thinner on one Edge than on the other, and are uled to pen up the Brick Pannels in Timber Buil - dings.. D dor on, was a Brick used by the An - cents of It Foot, or z Spans long, ( whence the Name ) and one Foot broad. This was the fm all eft fort of Brick used by the Greeks in their private Houses, for there was a larger fort in use in their publick Edifices, which they called,. Pen tadoron, which was foot Inches long, and Foot broad.. Same or Sandal Bricks, are such slie outmost in a Kiln or Clamp, and consequent - ly are Toft and useless as not being thoroughly burnt, u. Great Bricks are iz Inches long, broad, and thick. The Weight of one about Pound; so that will weigh, and of them Pound. Their Use is to build Fence Walls, together with, iz. Pilafier or But - tress Bricks, which are of the fame ) dimensions with them, only they have a Notch at one End of half the Breadth of the Brick. Their Use is to bind the Work at the Pilasters of Fence Walls which are built of great Bricks, - Paving Bricks or Tiles, these are of several Sizes in see - ral Counties and Places.. Place Bricks are such as are made in a Place made on purpose for them near the Building they are to be used in.. Statute or small common Bricks: These ought to be Inches long,. broad, and zf thick; of these usually weighs about Pound, and consequently, Pound, and about in Number are a Tun Weight; These are commonly used in paving of Cellars, Hearths, Sinks, &c. or a, if true Measure, will pave a Yard Square, and will pave a Square or Foot, laid flat; but if laid edge - wife, they must be double in Number. Bricks are burnt either in a Kiln or a Clamp: Those that are burnt in a ' Kiln, are first fet or pla -. ced in it, and then the Kiln being coygred with Pieces of Bricks, they first put in some great or cord Wood to dry the Ware with a gentle Fire, which is continued till the Ware is pretty dry; which they know by the Colour of the Smoaks turning from a whitifti Dark to a black transp - rent Smook; then they put in no more Wood, but proceed to burn the Bricks with Bush, Furze, Straw, - Heath, Brake or Fern Faggots, having first dam ’ d up the Mouth f the Kiln with their Shin - log as they call it ( which is Pieces of Bricks pi - led up one on another, and then closed up with wet Brick Earth instead of Mortar ) only leaving just Room to put in a Faggot: They then conti - nue to put in more and more Faggots, till they make the Kiln and its Arches look white with Heat, and that the Fire, begins to appear at the Top of the Kiln. Then they begin to flackenthe Fire for about half an Hour or an Hour, and so let all cool by Degrees. The Ware will be burnt usually in about Hours. But now - a - days about London, they usually burn Bricks in Clamps, which are built of the Bricks to be burnr, something after the manner of the Arches in Kilns, vi. with a Vacancy between each Brick ’ s Breadth, ( c. for the Fire to play through; but with this Difference, that instead of arching, they truss or span it over, by making the Bricks project one over another on both Sides the Place for the Wood and Coals to lie in, till they meet, and are bonded by the Bricks at the Top which elofes all up. The ' face for the Fuel is carried up strait on both Side ri a - bout Foot high, then they fill it alrnojt wi h Wood, and over that lay a Covering of Sea - coal; and then they over - span the Arch: But they drew Sea - coal also over at the Clamp, betwixt ail the Rows of Bricks; then they fire the Wood and then the Coal and when all is burnt out, they con - crude the Bricks burnt enough. building.c: BUILDING. There are some good Rules and Directions about Building which are given in Mox - onsMechanick. Exercises, and other Books of that kind, which ’ tis very proper every Gentleman shot ’ be acquainted with, that he may not be cheated or imposed upon by his Workmen: And those are such as these; First, with respect to the Foundation, Care ought to be taken, that after the Cellars are dug, if there be any, or if none, after the Trenches are dug in which rhe Walls are to stand, to try allthe Foundations either by a Crow, a Rammer, or which is best, with a Borer, such Well Diggers, Miners, use, whether they are throughly found, and are fit to bear rhe Weight that is to be laid upon them. If the Foundation be not very loose, it may be cured by ramming in great B U I great Stones with an heavy Rammer, the Stones being placed dole together, about a Foot wider on each Side of the Trench than the Breadth of the Wall is to be; but if it be so loose that this will not do, you must get good Pieces of Oak, whose Length must be the Breadth of the Trench, or about a Foot longer than the Breadth of the Wall, and these should be laid a cross the Foundation, about a Foot asunder, and being well ratnm ’ d down, lay long Planks upon them, which must be pinn ’ d down to them: And if this be not fuf - scient, Piles of a much greater Length must be driven down so deep till they reach good Ground, and then strong Planks pinn ’ d down to their Tops & c. If the Foundation be faulty only in Patches, there may Arches be turned over the insufficient Places, which will take oft ' the Weight from bear - ing upon them. And sometimes it may be proper to use inverted Arches. The Foundation being well secured, the next Gaffe is to fee that the Walls be all made of the fame Thickness as they are in the Design; for which Purpose, there should be Numbers to ex - press their Thickness in the Draft., The Walls alio must be well wrought. and hounded as they call it: In order to which the Mor - tar must be well made of good well burnt Lime and ( harp Sand; the usual Proportion, is a Load of Sand of Bufhels to a Hundred of Lime of a Buftiels, or a Bufliel of Lime to one and an half of Sand; but when the Sand is not very sharp, there must be a greater Proportion of it to the Lime. In Hacking of Lime Care shot ’ d be taken, that though it be witted every - where a little, yet it be not over - witted; arid every Layer or Bed of Lime should be covered with Sand to keep in the Steam, that it may not fly away, but be forced to mix k self with the Sand; and this will make the Mor - tar much stronger. The Mortar also must be well lenten with a Beater three or four times over be - fore ’ tis used, that the Knots of the Lime may be all broken, and the Lime and Sand mingled. very well together: And it will be still better, If after the first beating it be let lie three or four Days, and then let it be beat well over again when tis used. If the Bricks are laid in very hot dry Weather, and it be some small Piece of Work which you would have very strong, it will be worth while to dip every Brick as ’ tis laid in a Pan of Water; and it will be of good use in great Work to throw Wa - ter on the Walls, after the Bricks are laid, by a iVlrtcnburgh Syphon, or fomefuch way. And the Walls also should be covered in Summer Time, to keep them from drying too hastily, as well as in Winter Time from Rain, Snow, or Frost, which last is a great Enemy to all kinds of Mortar, e - specially to that which hath been newly witted. Let the Workmen also in doing up the Walls, not carry any one above three Foot high, before the next adjoining Wall is brought up equal with it, that so they may join together, and make good Bond in the Work. In the Middle of Walls Care should be taken that Joint is not laid on Joint, at least as seldom as may be, that good Bond may be made there as well as on the Outside. When Timber is laid on Brick - work, as Tor - felsfor Mantle Trees or Lintels for Windows, Templets for Girders, &c. let it be always laid in Loam, for that is a great Preserver of Timber, which Mortar will eat and corrode: The fame thing should be done with sce Ends f Joifts and Girders, some Workmen dab their End with Pitch, to preserve them from the Mortar.
